newsitem.title: CANADA: Prairie pork industry looks beyond U.S. for growth.
newsitem.headline: Prairie pork industry looks beyond U.S. for growth.

text.p: Canada's pork industry is expanding and exploring new routes to offshore markets as its main market, the United States, becomes more self-sufficient in meeting its own pork needs.
"The U.S. is becoming more and more self-sufficient in pork production so we have to look further afield," said Bill McLean, general manager of Winnipeg operations for Schneider Corp.
Canada sold C$488 million in fresh, chilled and frozen pork to the U.S. in 1995, Canada Pork International said.
Japan was the second largest consumer in 1995, buying C$205 million-worth, CPI said.
"North American consumption of pork is static, it runs in the area of 60 lbs (27 kgs) a person a year. World pork demand is growing at 30 million pigs a year," McLean said.
Mexico and Eastern Europe hold promising market potential, but the industry is looking to the East.
"I think the primary growth for Canadian pork exports will continue to be in Asia. Japan has had steady growth," Maple Leaf Foods International president Ted Bilyea told Reuters from Toronto.
But the distance to Asia could make what appear to be minor fluctuations in shipping costs into prohibitive rises.
"A quarter cent a pound over a year in our volume will make a difference in income of over C$1 million," McLean said.
In June Schneider started building a C$40-million hog kill plant in Winnipeg with a view to mainly supply Asian demand.

"For the overseas market, the cost of air shipping is much higher than by freight. We can store pork up to 40 days but once the package is opened, it tends to age faster, so for clients that are sensitive to that, it may be important," said Barry Prentice at University of Manitoba Transport Institute.
Logistics are also important, Schneider's McLean said.
"I have my product ready to go (by truck to Vancouver) four days before the ship sails for Japan. Although rail's cheaper, I'm not always guaranteed it'll make the ship on time," McLean said.

Despite transportation costs, Prairie pork should still be cost competitive. A large amount of feed grains are grown in the region and are likely to stay there now that rail subsidies have been discontinued.

"Japan's cost is three times ours to produce a pound of pork. Holland and Denmark have restricted land bases, we don't have that problem," said Gary Stott, manager of Elite Swine Inc, one of Manitoba's top hog marketers.
